unit.title: Plan to undertake a routine task

summary: This unit teaches you to plan a routine electrical task before you pick up a tool. You will learn to read a job card, a drawing and a specification, break the task into safe steps, and work out the tools, materials, people and time it needs. You will also learn to plan for hazards, agree the plan with your supervisor, deal with changes, and check, finish and report the work.

blocks.p: A **routine task** is one that is done often, in the usual way: changing a light fitting, adding an outlet, replacing a breaker, fixing a security light. Because the job is familiar, it is easy to start without thinking. Most problems on routine jobs come from poor planning: the wrong materials, a missed step, a circuit nobody isolated, or a customer who was not told the power would be off.

This unit is for Level 2 trainees in Electrical Installation and Maintenance who work under supervision. You are not expected to price jobs or run a site. You are expected to understand the job, plan your part of it safely and clearly, and tell your supervisor when something does not fit the plan.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Read the job card or work order and pick out what is to be done, where, by when and to what standard. Ask about anything that is unclear, and write the answer down.
Find and use the right information
Use the drawings, the specification, the maker's instructions and the Centre's procedures, and make sure each one is the latest version.
Break the task into steps in a safe, sensible order, with checks along the way and safe isolation before any electrical work.
Plan the tools, materials and people
Work out from the drawing what is needed, check that it is available and in good condition, and know who does each part.
Spot the hazards of each step and choose the controls before work starts; record them on a risk assessment.
Estimate how long each step takes, make a simple schedule, and keep to the deadline or warn your supervisor early.
Agree the plan with your supervisor, brief your team and tell the people who will be affected.
Stop, make safe and report when something unexpected happens, then update the plan.
Check the work against the job card, clean up, complete the report, and note what to plan differently next time.

flow: Receive the job card
Understand the task
Gather the information
Plan the steps, resources, safety and time
Agree the plan with your supervisor
Do the work, checking as you go
Finish, clean up and report
Review the plan for next time

blocks.note: Electrical work in Jamaica must meet the electrical code, which is based on the US National Electrical Code (NEC). New installations, and larger alterations, are inspected and certified before JPS will connect or reconnect them; the **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)** oversees this. Your supervisor will tell you when a job needs inspection. Your plan should always show who will test the work and who will sign it off.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow a real job from the job card to the final report. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will show you the Centre's own job cards, risk assessment forms and schedules.
Every job starts with an instruction. On most sites it is written on a **job card** or **work order** (some firms call it a job sheet or work ticket). Read all of it before you plan anything.

blocks.h: What a job card tells you

head: Part of the job card
What it tells you
rows: A reference used for materials, time sheets, tests and the final report.
Customer or department, and a contact
Who asked for the work and who to speak to on site.
The building, floor, room or unit, for example 'Block C, Room 12'.
What must be done, for example 'Supply and fit two 110 V outlets on the north wall'.
When the work must be finished, or when it is allowed, for example 'Saturday only' or 'after 3 p.m.'.
The materials, the finish and the rules the work must meet.
Keys, access, permits, known hazards and people who must be told.
Who issued the job, who did it, and who checked and accepted it.

blocks.note: A short line at the bottom of a job card, such as 'Tenant works nights: no drilling before 1 p.m.', can change your whole plan. Read every line, including the small print.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **specification** tells you which materials and equipment to use and how well the finished work must be done. The **quality standard** is the level the finished work must reach. Examples: 'outlets fixed level at the height shown on the drawing'; 'all cables in PVC conduit concealed in the wall'; 'LED battens, cool white, with the fixings the maker supplies'; 'all work to the electrical code'. If the job card and the specification say different things, ask before you buy or fit anything.

blocks.h: When something is unclear or does not agree

ul: If a detail is missing or unclear, ask the person who gave you the job, usually your supervisor. Write down the answer, the date and who told you.

If two documents disagree, for example the job card says three outlets and the drawing shows four, do not choose for yourself. Ask your supervisor which is right, and have the answer noted on the job card.
If the customer tells you something different from the job card, listen politely, note it and check with your supervisor before you change anything.
Never guess. A wrong guess costs time and materials, and on electrical work it can cost a life.

blocks.h: Know the limits of the job

blocks.p: The job card sets the **scope** of the work: what you have been asked, and allowed, to do. Extra work that nobody approved may be unsafe, may not be paid for, may not be covered by the inspection, and may be outside what you are authorised to do.

head: Situation
Right response
rows: The customer asks for an extra outlet while you are there
Be polite, note the request and pass it to your supervisor. Extra work may need a new job card, materials, time and a price.
You find a fault that is not part of your job, such as a scorched terminal in the panel
Do not touch it or try to fix it. Keep the area safe and report it to your supervisor at once.
An item in the specification is not available
Report it. Do not swap in something different without approval: a different size or rating may be unsafe or not to specification.
You think the job card is wrong
Say so to your supervisor before you start, and explain why.

blocks.p: The job card tells you what to do. Other documents tell you where, with what and how. Collect them before you plan, and check that each one is the latest version.

head: Source
What it tells you
What to check
rows: What, where, by when, for whom, and to what standard
Read all of it and ask about gaps
Drawings: layout (floor plan), wiring and circuit diagrams
Where each item goes, cable routes, which circuit feeds what
Latest revision; legend; scale; written dimensions
Materials, sizes, ratings, finishes and standards
That it agrees with the job card and the drawing
How to fix, connect and use the equipment; fixing heights; tools needed; clearances
Read them before you order and again before you fit
Safe work procedures and the Centre's safety rules
The safe way to do a task, such as safe isolation or using a stepladder
The minimum safety rules for installations
Your instructor or supervisor shows you the parts that apply
Labels can be wrong: always prove dead at the point of work
Supervisor, experienced workers and the customer
Answers, local knowledge, access, working hours
Write down what you are told

head: Part of the drawing
What it shows
rows: The title, drawing number, scale, date, who drew and checked it, and the revision letter or number.
What each symbol means. Always read it: the same item can be drawn in different ways by different designers.
How many times smaller the drawing is than the real thing, for example 1:50.
What was changed, when and by whom. The highest revision is normally the current one.
Heights, cable types, mounting details and other instructions.
Written measurements. A written dimension is more reliable than a measurement taken off the paper.

blocks.p: Symbols vary between drawings: US-style and British-style drawings are both used in Jamaica. The legend is always the final word.

head: Item
Often drawn as
rows: A small circle, sometimes with a cross inside
The letter S on US-style drawings (S3 for a two-way switch, which US catalogues call a three-way switch), or a small circle with a short line on British-style drawings
A circle with two short parallel lines on US-style drawings; a small half-circle or box on British-style drawings
A rectangle, often shaded or hatched
Lines between the points; the legend says what each line style means

blocks.h: Working out real lengths from the scale

blocks.p: A scale of **1:50** means 1 mm on the drawing is 50 mm in real life. To find a real length, measure on the drawing and multiply by the scale number. To change millimetres to metres, divide by 1,000.

blocks.note: A drawing is only to scale when it is printed at its proper size. A copy that has been reduced, or a drawing viewed on a phone, is not to scale. Use the written dimensions where they are given, and never measure a drawing marked 'Do not scale'.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Designs change. A socket may have been moved, or a circuit added, since your copy was printed. Check the revision letter or number against the list your supervisor keeps. Mark old copies 'superseded' and take them off the job, so nobody works from them by mistake.

sections.title: Planning the steps and the method

blocks.p: Breaking a task into steps helps you work in order and miss nothing. It puts the safety steps in the right place, lets you estimate the time, share the work out and check progress.

ul: **Prepare first:** information, materials, tools, access, and telling the people affected.
**Make safe before you touch:** safe isolation comes before any cover is removed or any conductor is touched.
**Remove before you fit:** take out the old item before fixing the new one.
**Rough work before neat work:** fix boxes and run cables before fitting accessories and covers.
**Group work by area:** finish one room or one floor before moving on, to save trips.
**Plan checks along the way**, then testing, restoring the supply, a final check that it works, clean-up and the report.

blocks.h: Example: replacing a fluorescent fitting with an LED batten

ol: Read the job card and the maker's sheet; check that the new batten matches the specification (length, power, colour of light, fixings).
Tell the room's users when the lights will be off.
Collect the tools, materials, PPE, a non-conducting stepladder, a voltage tester and proving unit, and a lock and tag.
Set up the stepladder and a barrier below the work area.
Identify the circuit; switch off, lock off and tag.
Prove the tester, prove the fitting dead between every pair of conductors, and prove the tester again.
Take down the diffuser and the old fitting, noting how it was connected. Keep the tubes whole.
Check the cable, the fixing points and the ceiling for damage.
Fix the new batten and connect the line, neutral and grounding (earth) conductors as the maker shows.
Check: terminals tight, no bare copper showing, ground connected, fitting secure. Ask your supervisor to look before the cover goes on.
Testing as the Centre's rules say; the person who locked off removes the lock and restores the supply; check the light works.
Clean up; store the old tubes for proper disposal; complete the job card and report.

blocks.note: Old fluorescent tubes and compact fluorescent lamps contain a small amount of mercury. Do not break them or throw them in the ordinary bin: keep them whole and store them for disposal as the Centre or the customer directs.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Plan a check wherever a mistake would be hard to put right later: before a wall is chased, before cables are covered, before covers go on, and before the supply is restored. Checking box positions against the drawing before you drill takes two minutes; moving a box after the wall is finished takes hours. These planned stopping points are sometimes called **hold points**: the work does not go on until the check is done.

A **method statement** is a written description of how a job will be done safely: the steps in order, the hazards and controls, the people, the plant and equipment, and the checks. Bigger sites ask for one before work starts. On small jobs a **job sheet** with the steps, materials, hazards and times does the same work.

ul: Do the jobs that need the same circuit switched off together, so the customer loses power only once.
Start with the job that has the earliest deadline, or the one other trades are waiting for.
Group the jobs by floor or area, so you carry tools and the ladder as few times as possible.
Plan noisy or dusty work for when the rooms are empty.
Keep tools and materials at hand, but out of walkways, doorways and stairs.
Leave a clear, level place for the stepladder.
Choose a safe spot for removed parts and waste.
Keep fire exits, the fire extinguisher and the panel clear.
Put up barriers and signs where other people pass.

blocks.p: **Resources** are everything the job needs: materials, tools and test instruments, PPE, people, time, access, transport and information. Plan them all; a missing tester or a locked door stops a job as surely as missing cable.

flow: Read the job card and the specification
Count the items on the drawing: outlets, switches, boxes, fittings
Measure each run on the drawing and use the scale
Add an allowance for connections and waste (often about 10%)
Round up to whole lengths, rolls and packs
Write the list: item, type and size, quantity, unit

head: Item
Type and size
Quantity
Unit
rows: As the specification says, for example 12 AWG copper with a grounding conductor
To suit the saddles and boxes

blocks.p: **Worked example.** On a 1:50 drawing, three cable runs measure 46 mm, 70 mm and 58 mm. Total on the drawing: 46 + 70 + 58 = 174 mm. Real length: 174 × 50 = 8,700 mm = 8.7 m. Add 10%: 8.7 × 0.1 = 0.87 m, so 8.7 + 0.87 = 9.57 m. Round up: take 10 m.
**Packs.** A job needs 140 cable clips and they come in packs of 50. 140 ÷ 50 = 2.8, so order 3 packs. You cannot buy 0.8 of a pack.

blocks.note: Always round up, never down. Running short in the middle of a job costs far more in time and travel than a few spare clips.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Go through your list of steps and write down the tools each step needs. A routine electrical task often needs:

ul: Insulated screwdrivers, side cutters, wire strippers, a cable knife or sheath stripper, long-nose pliers
Tape measure, spirit level, pencil or marker, drill with suitable bits, wall plugs and fixings
A non-conducting (fibreglass) stepladder
A two-pole voltage tester and its proving unit, and a lock-off kit: lockout device, personal padlock and danger tag
The test instruments for whoever does the tests, such as a continuity and insulation resistance tester
PPE, a torch, a dust sheet, rubbish bags and a vacuum or brush

head: What to check
What to look for
rows: Hand and power tools (pre-use visual inspection)
Cracked or loose handles, damaged insulation, blunt or chipped bits, frayed power cords, missing guards
Undamaged leads and probes, a good battery, a correct reading on the proving unit, in date if they are calibrated
Sound feet, rungs and locking bars, readable labels; fibreglass for electrical work
Check against the materials list and the delivery note: right items, sizes and quantities, nothing damaged

blocks.p: Report a shortage, a wrong item or a damaged tool to your supervisor straight away. Do not swap in something else: a different cable size, breaker rating or fitting may be unsafe or not to the specification. The supervisor may change the order of the work, send for the right item or move the job to another day.

ul: **People:** how many, with which skills, and who does each part. Only an authorised, competent person does the tests.
**Time:** how long each step takes and when the work is allowed (see the section on scheduling).
**Access:** keys, security passes, opening hours, parking, and whether a room will be in use.
**Transport:** getting people, ladders and materials to site.
**Permits and permissions:** some sites need a permit for hot work, working at height or switching off a supply. Your supervisor arranges these.

blocks.p: Plan safety before work starts, so that the controls are ready before anyone is at risk. A hazard found while you are up a ladder with your hands in a fitting is found too late.
A **hazard** is anything that could cause harm. A **risk** is how likely that harm is and how bad it would be.

head: Hazard
Example
Control to put in the plan
rows: Changing a light fitting or an outlet
Safe isolation: switch off, lock off, tag, prove dead with a tester proved before and after. Never work live.
A sound non-conducting stepladder, set up correctly, with someone to foot it; or a mobile platform for longer work
A screwdriver dropped from the ladder
A tool pouch; a barrier and sign below
Drilling a block wall for saddles
Check the tool; safety glasses, dust mask and ear protection; check for hidden cables and pipes first
Cutting a chase in a wall
Dust mask and ear defenders; do it when the building is empty; clean up with a vacuum
Carrying a cable drum or a long batten
Lift correctly, get help, use a trolley
Off-cuts and leads on the floor
Keep the area tidy; route leads away from walkways
Tell them; barriers and signs; keep them clear of the work
A hot roof space in the afternoon sun
Work there early in the day, take water and breaks
Handle and store them as the Centre directs

flow: List the steps of the task
For each step, ask what could go wrong and who could be hurt
Decide how likely it is and how bad it would be
Choose controls, best first
Write it down
Brief the team, and review it if anything changes

blocks.p: A **high** risk must be reduced before the work starts. A **medium** risk needs controls and someone keeping an eye on it. A **low** risk needs normal care. Many centres and firms use a number scale instead (for example 1 to 5 for each, multiplied together); the idea is the same.
Choose controls from the top of this list down. PPE is the last line of defence, never the first.

head: Level
Example on a routine electrical task
rows: Work dead: isolate, lock off and prove dead, so there is nothing live to touch.
Battery tools instead of mains tools; a platform instead of a ladder.
Barriers, guards, panel covers, a GFCI (RCD) on the extension lead.
Safe isolation procedure, permits, signs, training, working when the room is empty.
Safety boots, safety glasses, gloves, dust mask, ear protection.

blocks.h: Safe isolation in every electrical plan

flow: Identify the circuit from the drawing and panel schedule
Tell the people affected
Switch off
Lock off with your own padlock and keep the key
Fix a danger tag
Prove your tester on the proving unit
Prove dead at the point of work, between every pair of conductors
Prove the tester again
Start work

blocks.note: Your plan must never include live work. If someone says a job cannot be done with the circuit dead, it is not a Level 2 task: tell your supervisor.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Listing the PPE in the plan means it is on site and worn from the start: safety boots, safety glasses, work gloves, a hard hat where needed, a dust mask, ear protection, and long sleeves in cotton or flame-resistant fabric. The plan should also say where the first-aid kit and the nearest suitable fire extinguisher (CO2 or dry powder) are, who the first-aider is, how to switch off the main supply, and the emergency numbers: **110** for ambulance and fire, **119** for police.

A time estimate tells everyone how long the job should take. It lets your supervisor plan other work, tells the customer how long the power will be off, and shows whether the job can be finished by the **deadline**.

ul: List the steps in order and estimate each one.
Use real times from past jobs, ask experienced workers, and read the maker's guide.
Do not forget the steps that are easy to leave out: travel, setting up, safe isolation, waiting for others, testing, clean-up and paperwork.
Add a sensible allowance for problems. On a small job, an extra 10 to 15 per cent is common.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** The steps take 25 min, 40 min, 1 h 10 min and 35 min, and clean-up takes 20 min. Change everything to minutes: 25 + 40 + 70 + 35 + 20 = 190 min. Change back: 190 ÷ 60 = 3 remainder 10, so 3 h 10 min. Add about 10% (19 min) for problems: plan for about 3 h 30 min.

blocks.note: Add up in minutes, then change to hours and minutes at the end. Remember that 1 h 10 min is 70 minutes, not 110.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **schedule** shows the order of the steps, when each one starts and finishes, and who does it. The simplest is a table; a **bar chart** (also called a Gantt chart) shows the same thing as bars against a time line, so overlaps and gaps are easy to see.

head: Step
Who
Start
Finish
rows: Set up and tell the office staff
Isolate, lock off and prove dead

blocks.p: To draw a bar chart, list the steps down the left side and the times across the top. Draw a bar for each step from its start to its finish, and write the person's name on it.

ul: Work backwards from the deadline to find the latest time you can start.
Plan around the customer: a school after classes or on Saturday, an office after hours, a shop before opening.
Tell the customer when the power will be off and for how long.
Allow for the time of year: rain in the rainy seasons and storms in the hurricane season stop outdoor work.

blocks.p: When more than one person works on a job, the plan shows who does each step and when. Check that two people will not need the same ladder or tool at the same time, and that each person is trained and authorised for their part. Some steps can be done at the same time, such as one person fixing boxes while another prepares the fittings on the floor, but nobody works on any conductor until the circuit is isolated and proved dead.

ul: Compare progress with the schedule at set times, for example at each break.
If the job is slipping, tell your supervisor as soon as you know, not at the deadline.
Never catch up by rushing, leaving out a test or skipping a safety step.
Agree a new finish time and tell the customer.

sections.title: Communicating the plan and handling changes

blocks.p: A plan works only when the right people know it. Each person needs different information.

head: Who
What they need to know
rows: The steps, method, materials, time, hazards and controls. The supervisor checks the plan, agrees changes and approves it before you start.
The steps, who does what, the hazards and controls, the PPE, the isolation points and what to do in an emergency.
When the work will happen, which rooms or circuits will be off and for how long, what they must do (save computer work, unplug equipment, keep clear), and when it is finished.
Where you will be working, when the power will be off, shared ladders, scaffold or access.
Which materials are needed, and when.

blocks.p: A **toolbox talk** is a short meeting, often 5 to 10 minutes, at the start of a shift or a job. The team goes over the tasks, the hazards and controls, the PPE, who does what, and the emergency arrangements. Everyone can ask questions. Many firms keep a record of who attended.

ul: Use plain words and give one step at a time.
Say why, not only what: people remember a reason.
Show the person if it helps.
Check understanding: ask them to tell you back what they will do.
Write down key figures, such as circuit numbers, sizes and heights.
Do not shout instructions across a noisy site or send them after the person has started.

blocks.h: When something changes or goes wrong

flow: Stop
Make the area safe; keep the circuit isolated and locked off
Tell your supervisor at once
Agree what to do
Update the plan and the times
Tell the team and the customer
Record the change on the job card

head: What happens
What to do
rows: Material out of stock, or the wrong item delivered
Report it; do not substitute; the supervisor decides.
An unexpected fault, such as damaged cable in a wall or a scorched terminal
Do not cover it up or fix it without approval; keep it isolated; report it.
Stop using it, tag it and replace it. Repeat any test done with a tester that later failed.
The job is taking longer than planned
Tell your supervisor early; do not leave out steps to save time.
Stop outdoor electrical work; switch to indoor work if the plan allows, or reschedule.
The supervisor re-plans. Do not take on work you are not trained or authorised to do.
The customer asks for extra work
Note it and refer it to your supervisor before agreeing to anything.

blocks.note: Check the forecast from the Meteorological Service of Jamaica when you plan outdoor work, especially in the rainy seasons (roughly May to June and September to November) and the hurricane season (June to November). Wet conditions and electrical work do not mix.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Check against
What to check
rows: Every item asked for is done, and nothing extra was done without approval.
Positions, heights and routes are as shown.
The right materials, ratings and fixings; connections as the maker shows.
Accessories firm, level and neat; covers on; no bare copper showing; cables supported; no damage to the building; area tidy.
Done by a competent person, passed, and the results recorded.

blocks.p: Use a **checklist** and tick each item off as you check it. Put right anything you find, or report it if you cannot. Then ask your supervisor to inspect the work and sign it off.

ul: Clean the work area: remove off-cuts, dust and packaging, and sort the waste (scrap copper, general waste, items such as old tubes that need special disposal).
Count your tools, so none is left in a ceiling, a box or a panel.
Return tools clean, and report and tag any that were damaged.
Return unused materials to the store and book them in.
Take down barriers and signs.
The supply is restored only after the checks and tests, by the person who locked it off.
Tell the customer or the building users that the work is finished, and explain anything they need to know, such as how to test and reset a GFCI outlet.

head: Include
Example
rows: Replaced four fluorescent fittings with four LED battens
As recorded on the test sheet, all passed
Planned 3 h 30 min; actual 4 h 05 min
Problems and how they were solved
One ceiling fixing was loose: refixed with new plugs
Anything found or still to do
Outlet behind the door is scorched: reported for a new job card

blocks.p: Write facts, not opinions. 'The east wall was hollow plasterboard, so hollow-wall fixings were needed' helps the next planner; 'the wall was terrible' does not.

After the job, compare what happened with what you planned. Which steps took longer? What was missing from the materials list? What worked well? Write the lessons down and use them on the next plan. A review is about improving the next job, not blaming anyone.

blocks.note: Keep a notebook of the real times for jobs you do often. After a few jobs your estimates will be far better than a guess.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain what a routine task is and why even routine jobs must be planned.
I can read a job card and pick out the task, the place, the deadline and the standard.
I can say what to do when information is missing, or when two documents disagree.
I can explain what the scope of a job is, and what to do about extra requests and faults outside the job.
I can name the sources of information for a task and say what each one tells me.
I can read a title block and a legend, and check that a drawing is the latest revision.
I can work out real lengths from a drawing's scale.
I can break a task into steps in a safe, sensible order, with safe isolation and checks along the way.
I can make a materials list with an allowance, rounded up to whole lengths and packs.
I can list the tools and instruments for a task and check them before use.
I can do a simple risk assessment and choose controls from the hierarchy of control.
I can estimate the time for a task, add up the times and draw a simple schedule.
I can say who needs to know about the plan, and lead or take part in a toolbox talk.
I can say what to do when something changes or goes wrong during a task.
I can check finished work against the job card, drawing and specification.
I can finish a task properly and write a completion report.
I can review a plan and use the lessons next time.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: 1 mm on the drawing = 50 mm in real life
A common allowance on cable and conduit for connections and waste
Lengths, rolls and packs are always rounded up
Add times in minutes, then change to hours and minutes
A common time allowance for problems on a small job
Ambulance and fire / police in Jamaica

terms: A schedule that shows each step as a bar against a time line.
A written list of items ticked off one by one so nothing is missed.
A record of what was done, the materials, the results, the time taken and any problems.
The latest date or time by which a task must be finished.
A planned stop where the work is checked before it goes on.
The document that says what job to do, where, for whom and by when.
The part of a drawing that explains its symbols.
A list of the items needed for a job, with the type, size and amount of each; also called a bill of materials.
A written description of how a job will be done safely, step by step.
A visual inspection of a tool or instrument before it is used.
How well the finished work must be done.
Everything a job needs: materials, tools, people, time, access, transport and information.
A numbered or lettered change to a drawing or document; the latest revision is the one to use.
How likely a hazard is to cause harm, and how serious the harm would be.
A written check of the hazards of a task and how each will be controlled.
A task that is done often, in the usual way.
The ratio between a length on a drawing and the real length, such as 1:50.
A plan that shows the order of the steps and when each will be done.
What the job includes, and so what you are asked and allowed to do.
The order in which the steps of a task are done.
A document that gives the materials, equipment and quality needed.
The box on a drawing with its title, number, scale, date and revision.
A short meeting at the start of a shift or job to go over the tasks and hazards.

c1.title: Veranda lights at a Montego Bay guest house
c1.text: Trainee Kerry-Ann Walters gets a job card from her supervisor, Mr Lloyd Bennett: 'Job 2217. Guest house, Montego Bay. Replace 6 veranda wall lights with weatherproof LED bulkhead fittings to the attached specification. Work between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. only. Complete by Friday.' The layout drawing in the job folder is Revision A and shows 7 wall lights. The guest house manager has a newer copy of the same drawing marked Revision C.

c2.title: Outlets for a church hall in Old Harbour
c2.text: Trainees Jordan Campbell and Shantelle Reid must list the materials for four new 110 V outlets along one wall of a church hall in Old Harbour, St Catherine, fed in surface PVC conduit. The drawing is at a scale of 1:50. On it, the route from the existing junction box to the first outlet measures 62 mm, and the runs between the outlets measure 48 mm, 48 mm and 52 mm. Their supervisor says to allow 10% extra on conduit and cable. Conduit comes in 3 m lengths, and saddles in packs of 25.

c3.title: LED battens in a Morant Bay school
c3.text: Supervisor Mr Desmond Ellis and trainees Akeem Brown and Tamara Hylton will replace eight old fluorescent fittings with LED battens in two classrooms at a primary school in Morant Bay, St Thomas. Both rooms' lights are on one circuit. Their plan allows: travel and set-up 30 min; isolate and prove dead 15 min; remove old fittings 60 min; fix and connect the battens 120 min; testing and restoring the supply 30 min; clean-up and handover 25 min. The principal will open the school on Saturday so the rooms are ready for Monday.

c4.title: Changes on the day at an Ocho Rios pharmacy
c4.text: Trainee Ricardo Thompson and electrician Ms Karen McKenzie are adding a new 20 A circuit and outlet for a medicine fridge at a pharmacy in Ocho Rios, St Ann. With the panel isolated, they take off its cover and find a scorched, loose conductor on the neutral bar from another circuit. The pharmacist then asks Ricardo to 'just put another outlet by the counter while you are here'. The store has sent 14 AWG cable, but the job card and drawing call for 12 AWG.

c5.title: Handing over an office job in Savanna-la-Mar
c5.text: Trainee Sasha-Gaye Brown has fitted three new outlets in an insurance office in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. The plan allowed 3 hours, but the job took 4, because the east wall turned out to be hollow plasterboard instead of block and needed different fixings. All three outlets work. Two outlet boxes and about 5 m of cable are left over. Her supervisor, Mr Patrick Grant, will inspect and sign off the job this afternoon.

questions.q: The job card says 6 lights, but Kerry-Ann's drawing shows 7. What should she do?
o: Fit 7, because a drawing always has more detail than a job card
Ask Mr Bennett which is right and note his answer on the card
Fit 6 now and come back for the seventh if anyone complains
Ask the guest house cleaner, who knows the veranda best
questions.why: When documents disagree, the person who issued the job decides, not the worker. Ask the supervisor, and record the answer on the job card so there is no argument later.

questions.q: Which copy of the layout drawing should Kerry-Ann plan from?
o: Revision A, because it is the copy that Mr Bennett put in the folder
Either copy, since both show the same veranda and lights
Revision C, once Mr Bennett confirms that it is the current one
Neither: she should measure the veranda and draw her own
questions.why: A later revision means the design has changed since Revision A. Plan from the newest issue, but confirm with the supervisor that it is the current, approved drawing, and take the old copy off the job.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann estimates the job at 7 hours of work. How should she schedule it?
o: Over two days, inside the 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. time window
In one long day from 7 a.m., so the job is finished sooner
In the evenings, when the guests are back and can be told
All on Friday, so the lights are new for the weekend guests
questions.why: The time window allows 5 hours a day, so 7 hours needs two days inside it, with the deadline still met. Starting early or working evenings breaks the customer's rules, and leaving it all to Friday leaves no time for problems.

questions.q: Where should Kerry-Ann look to find exactly which bulkhead fittings to buy?
o: In the title block of the layout drawing
In the specification attached to the job card
In the legend beside the drawing's symbols
On the delivery note from the last hardware order
questions.why: The specification gives the materials and equipment: type, rating, finish and so on. The title block identifies the drawing, and the legend explains its symbols; neither tells you which fitting to buy.

questions.q: What is the real length of the whole route, before any allowance is added?
questions.why: Add the drawing lengths: 62 + 48 + 48 + 52 = 210 mm. Multiply by the scale: 210 × 50 = 10,500 mm, which is 10.5 m.

questions.q: With the 10% allowance, how many 3 m lengths of conduit should go on the list?
o: 3 lengths
5 lengths
12 lengths
4 lengths
questions.why: 10.5 m plus 10% is 11.55 m. 11.55 ÷ 3 = 3.85, which must be rounded up to 4 whole lengths. Three lengths give only 9 m.

questions.q: The plan needs 34 saddles. What should the materials list show?
o: 1 pack, since 34 is close to the 25 in a pack
1.36 packs, the exact amount that the job needs
34 packs, so that each saddle is counted
2 packs, rounding up to whole packs
questions.why: 34 ÷ 25 = 1.36, and you cannot buy part of a pack, so round up to 2 packs (50 saddles). One pack would leave the job 9 saddles short.

questions.q: The conduit arrives as 25 mm, but the list said 20 mm. What should Jordan and Shantelle do?
o: Fit it, since bigger conduit holds the cables more easily
Tell their supervisor before any of it is cut or fixed
Fit it, but buy 25 mm saddles and boxes themselves
Send it all back and leave the job until next month
questions.why: Check every delivery against the list and report any difference before using it. The 25 mm conduit will not fit the 20 mm boxes, saddles and fittings; the supervisor decides whether to exchange it or change the plan.

questions.q: How long is Mr Ellis's plan in total?
o: 3 h 40 min
4 h 40 min
4 h 20 min
5 h 40 min
questions.why: Add in minutes: 30 + 15 + 60 + 120 + 30 + 25 = 280 min. 280 ÷ 60 = 4 remainder 40, so 4 h 40 min.

questions.q: Akeem and Tamara will work in different rooms, but on the same circuit. How should the isolation be planned?
o: Each person fits a padlock to a multi-lock hasp
Mr Ellis fits one padlock for the team and keeps the only key
One danger tag with all three names on it is enough
The breaker is switched off and the panel door is closed
questions.why: Everyone working on a circuit fits their own lock, usually on a multi-lock hasp, so the breaker cannot be switched on until the last person has finished and removed theirs. A tag or a closed door cannot stop anyone.

questions.q: What should the plan say about the old fluorescent tubes?
o: Break them into the skip so they take up less room
Leave them in the classroom for the school to throw out
Remove them whole and store them for proper disposal
Put them in the ordinary bin with the cardboard boxes
questions.why: Fluorescent tubes contain a small amount of mercury. Keep them whole and store them safely for disposal as the Centre or the customer directs; never break them or put them in ordinary waste.

questions.q: After 90 minutes on the fixing step, only 3 of the 8 battens are up. At this rate, how much longer than planned will that step take?
o: About 30 minutes more
About 1 hour more
About 3 hours more
About 2 hours more
questions.why: 3 battens in 90 minutes is 30 minutes each. 8 battens × 30 min = 240 min, against 120 min planned: 120 minutes, or 2 hours, more. The supervisor should know now, so the finish time can be re-planned.

questions.q: What should Ricardo do about the scorched conductor on the neutral bar?
o: Point it out to Ms McKenzie and leave it for her decision
Tighten it while the panel is off, as it will save a call-out
Leave it alone and say nothing, as it is not his circuit
Wrap it in tape so that the scorching cannot spread
questions.why: A fault outside your job is reported, not fixed on your own and not ignored. A scorched, loose neutral can overheat and start a fire, so the supervisor needs to know at once; she will decide what to do and record it.

questions.q: How should Ricardo answer the pharmacist's request for an extra outlet?
o: Fit it at once, since the panel is already switched off
Refuse firmly, as customers may not change a job card
Note it, and say Ms McKenzie must agree it with them first
Fit it, and add the cost to the bill later without telling
questions.why: Extra work needs approval: it may need a new job card, materials, time, a price and its own testing. Be polite, write the request down and refer it to the supervisor.

questions.q: Why must the 14 AWG cable not be used for the new circuit?
o: It is thinner than 12 AWG and is not rated for a 20 A breaker
It is thicker than 12 AWG and will not fit the outlet's terminals
14 AWG may be used on 220 V circuits only, not on 110 V circuits
AWG cable is not allowed under the specification for a fridge
questions.why: In AWG, the bigger the number, the thinner the wire: 14 AWG is thinner than 12 AWG. On copper, 14 AWG is protected at no more than 15 A, so it would overheat on a 20 A circuit. Follow the specification and report the wrong delivery.

questions.q: Mr Grant asks Sasha-Gaye how she knows the job is complete. What is the best evidence?
o: The outlets work, and the office staff seem pleased with them
The job took longer than planned, so it must be thorough
The office manager has not reported any problems so far
Each job card item ticked off, and the tests recorded
questions.why: Completion is shown against the job card, the drawing and the specification, with the tests done and recorded. An outlet that works can still have a loose terminal or a missing ground.

questions.q: Which sentence belongs in Sasha-Gaye's completion report?
o: Took 4 h, not 3: east wall was plasterboard, so new fixings
The job went fine in the end, and no other details are needed
The plan was wrong as usual, so of course the job ran over
Outlets fitted and working; customer happy with the result
questions.why: A report records facts: what was done, the time planned and taken, and the reason for any difference. That helps the next planner; vague comments and blame do not.

questions.q: What should Sasha-Gaye do with the two spare boxes and the 5 m of cable?
o: Keep them in her tool bag for the next job
Leave them with the office manager to store
Return them to the store and book them in
Throw them out with the boxes and packaging
questions.why: Unused materials go back to the store and are booked in, so the job's costs are right and the items can be used again. Keeping them or giving them away leaves the records wrong.

questions.q: A detail drawing at a scale of 1:20 shows a box 65 mm from a door frame. How far is it from the frame in real life?
questions.why: Multiply the drawing length by the scale number: 65 × 20 = 1,300 mm, which is 1.3 m. Dividing by 20 instead of multiplying is a common mistake.

questions.q: On a risk matrix, a hazard is rated 'likely' with 'major' harm. What should happen before the work starts?
o: Start as planned, but take extra care during that step
Reduce the risk with better controls before work begins
Ask the most experienced worker to do that step alone
Record it on the form and review it at the end of the job
questions.why: A high risk must be brought down with controls, chosen from the top of the hierarchy, before anyone starts. Taking care or leaving it to one person does not change the risk.
